10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Presenting the data at a global and annual scale reduces the uncertainty and variability inherent in SST measurements, and therefore the reconstruction of observed data is considered to be a good representation of global SST. This data set covers the Earth’s oceans with sufficient frequency and resolution to ensure that overall averages are not inappropriately distorted by singular events or missing data due to sparse in situ measurements or cloud cover. Figure 1 of EPA’s Sea Surface Temperature indicator shows a confidence interval that indicates the degree of accuracy associated with the estimates over time. As the technical documentation for that indicator explains, the ERSST reconstruction yields results that are similar to other reconstructions using alternative methods.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

The observed and projected time series cover the same spatial extent—the entire global ocean—and the same indicator definition. However, they are fundamentally based on different pixel sizes for analysis.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Sea Surface Temperature indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. One such factor is that anomalies are also dampened when and where data were too sparse for a reliable reconstruction. Data screening results in loss of multiple observations at latitudes higher than 60 degrees north or south. Effects of screening at high latitudes are minimal in the context of the global average; the main effect is to lessen anomalies and widen confidence intervals.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below. SST is influenced by multiple systems and processes, so it may be less direct to model than, say, surface air temperature.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. The ERSST model has largely corrected for measurement error, but some uncertainty still exists. Contributing factors include variations in sampling methodology by era as well as geographic region, and instrument error from buoys and ships. Figure 1 of EPA’s Sea Surface Temperature indicator includes a confidence interval, which is associated with the biases and errors in the measurements and treatments of the data. For each year, the one-sigma error provided by NOAA was multiplied by 1.96 to approximate a 95 percent confidence interval. The resulting values were added to or subtracted from the reported anomaly to define the upper and lower confidence bounds, respectively.

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

13. Sources of Variability

SST varies regionally, seasonally, and sometimes from year to year as a result of climate patterns such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Normalizing regional differences by calculating anomalies rather than using absolute temperatures.
  • Generating a global average.
  • Using annual averages.
  • Smoothing GCM outputs with an 11-year moving average.
